title: Complex Medical Dermatology Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Postgraduate physician-level independent education for dermatology-trained clinicians/trainees; not entry-level medical education.
assumedKnowledge: General immunology, infectious disease and pharmacology
prerequisites.notFor: Patient-specific diagnosis or treatment; unsupervised procedures, prescribing, inpatient management, or credentialing.

objectives: Build a prioritized differential for severe or complex eruptions using morphology, chronology, host context and acuity.
Select and interpret biopsy, DIF, microbiology, serology and systemic evaluation proportionately.
Recognize high-risk drug eruptions, mucosal disease, infection, transplant complications and systemic inflammatory clues requiring prompt clinician/team assessment.
Evaluate medical dermatologic treatment choices against current guideline sources, comorbidities, contraindications and monitoring requirements.
Communicate diagnostic uncertainty and coordinate with oncology, rheumatology, transplant, infectious disease, pathology and wound-care teams.
Use authentic linked case imagery ethically and avoid exporting or rehosting patient material.

units.title: Complex dermatology consultation: morphology, acuity, and systems review
objectives: Construct a concise skin-focused history and examination, using primary lesion morphology, distribution, tempo, symptoms, and mucosal involvement.
Identify physiologic instability, immunosuppression, fever, skin pain, rapidly progressive disease, and eye/mucosal involvement as escalation triggers.
State a prioritized differential and decide what information is needed before labeling the eruption.
topics: Morphology and distribution
Skin of color considerations
Medication/transplant/cancer history
Emergency triage and interdisciplinary handoff
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: diagnosis and clinical management (broad alignment; no fellowship blueprint published)
units.casePractice: Use a fictional referral vignette; build a one-line problem representation and red-flag checklist without premature etiologic closure.
units.assessment: Structured oral presentation: 4/5 points for morphology/tempo, systemic risk, medication/context and a safe next step; no unsupported diagnosis.

units.title: Diagnostic strategy, biopsy planning, pathology and immunofluorescence
objectives: Match lesion age and site to routine histology versus perilesional direct immunofluorescence (DIF) sampling.
Integrate clinical pattern, histology and serology while recognizing sampling and false-negative limitations.
Write a clinicopathologic question for the dermatopathologist.
topics: H&E and DIF specimen selection
Culture/PCR when infection is plausible
Serologic correlation
Repeat biopsy and clinicopathologic conference
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: diagnostic testing, dermatopathology and clinical reasoning
units.casePractice: Compare a fictional tense-blister presentation with a medication-related eruption; request the right paired specimens and explain why.
units.assessment: Specimen plan scored 0–2 each for lesion choice, DIF-site, test selection, differential and interpretation limits.

units.title: Autoimmune blistering disease and mucosal emergencies
objectives: Compare pemphigus, pemphigoid, linear IgA disease, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita and mimics at a syndrome level.
Use clinical findings with H&E/DIF and targeted serology rather than a single test.
Recognize extensive erosions, mucosal/ocular disease and infection as urgent escalation needs.
topics: Intraepidermal versus subepidermal split
DIF patterns and antigen testing
Mucosal disease
Therapy monitoring and infection risk
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: immunobullous disease, diagnosis, therapeutics, complications
units.casePractice: Interpret fictional histology text and DIF patterns; specify what remains unconfirmed and who must be consulted.
units.assessment: Five-item diagnostic sequence: morphology, biopsy, DIF, corroboration, safety/consultation; 1 point each.

units.title: Severe drug reactions and oncology-treatment toxicities
objectives: Build an exposure timeline including prescription, OTC, infusion and recently stopped agents.
Differentiate uncomplicated exanthem from high-risk patterns with blistering, mucosa, skin pain, facial edema, fever or organ involvement.
Coordinate urgent evaluation and treatment-hold decisions with the oncology/prescribing team; avoid unsupervised re-challenge.
topics: SJS/TEN and DRESS warning signs
Immune checkpoint inhibitor eruptions
Targeted therapy and cytotoxic patterns
Pharmacovigilance and multidisciplinary decisions
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: adverse effects, urgent dermatologic conditions and systems-based care
units.casePractice: A fictional patient on a checkpoint inhibitor reports a new blistering eruption; produce an escalation note and differential, not a drug-continuation order.
units.assessment: Safety checklist scored for drug timeline, severity flags, organ review, communication and uncertainty.

units.title: Cutaneous lupus, dermatomyositis and connective-tissue disease
objectives: Distinguish major cutaneous lupus patterns and identify features that prompt systemic evaluation.
Recognize dermatomyositis-pattern findings and associated systemic symptoms warranting coordinated evaluation.
Use skin findings as clues rather than as stand-alone proof of systemic disease.
topics: Acute/subacute/chronic cutaneous lupus
Photosensitivity and scarring
Dermatomyositis signs
Scleroderma and overlap syndromes
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: inflammatory disease, systemic associations and evidence-based management
units.casePractice: Compare fictional photodistributed eruptions and construct a targeted question list for primary care/rheumatology.
units.assessment: Short answer: morphology, differential, systemic questions and referral rationale; 4 domains, 0–2 points each.

units.title: Cutaneous vasculitis, panniculitis and neutrophilic dermatoses
objectives: Classify palpable purpura and other inflammatory lesions by morphology, distribution and timing.
Identify systemic red flags and select a proportionate laboratory/biopsy evaluation.
Differentiate inflammatory ulceration from infection and recognize pathergy risk in suspected pyoderma gangrenosum.
topics: Small-vessel vasculitis
Biopsy timing and DIF
Panniculitis patterns
Pyoderma gangrenosum and wound trauma
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: inflammatory disease, urgent evaluation, pathology and complications
units.casePractice: Use a fictional painful ulcer and palpable purpura case; list competing diagnoses and decide which finding changes urgency.
units.assessment: Differential matrix scored for distribution, systemic review, biopsy strategy, infection exclusion and safe wound handling.

units.title: Severe psoriasis, eczema and chronic inflammatory dermatoses
objectives: Assess inflammatory disease severity with extent, special sites, symptoms, functional burden and patient goals.
Screen for clinically important comorbidity and treatment-specific risks.
Compare topical, phototherapy and systemic/biologic options at a guideline level and identify when specialty coordination is required.
topics: Psoriasis severity and comorbidity
Atopic dermatitis and erythroderma
Hidradenitis suppurativa
Phototherapy and advanced therapeutics
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: inflammatory disease, therapeutics, adverse effects and preventive care
units.casePractice: A fictional adult with extensive plaque psoriasis and joint symptoms: produce a severity summary and comorbidity-screen plan.
units.assessment: Plan rubric: phenotype/severity, comorbidity, options, risks/monitoring, shared decision; 0–2 each.

units.title: Cutaneous complications of transplantation and immune dysregulation
objectives: Recognize acute and chronic cutaneous GVHD patterns in the appropriate transplant context while preserving differential diagnosis.
Distinguish GVHD from infection, medication eruption, engraftment-related conditions and malignancy.
Communicate urgency and coordinate with transplant clinicians; do not infer GVHD from morphology alone.
topics: Allogeneic HSCT context
Cutaneous GVHD phenotype and staging concepts
Biopsy limits
Infection and immunosuppression tradeoffs
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: immunology, transplant complications, infection and multidisciplinary care
units.casePractice: Fictional post-transplant rash: make a differential and outline what transplant-team information is needed before interpretation.
units.assessment: One-page consult note scored on timeline, distribution, differential, evaluation and team coordination.

units.title: Infectious dermatoses in medically complex and immunocompromised patients
objectives: Recognize common bacterial and fungal cutaneous infection patterns and atypical presentations in immunosuppression.
Select appropriate culture, microscopy, histology or molecular testing from the clinical question.
Avoid anchoring infection or inflammatory disease before safety-critical alternatives are considered.
topics: Bacterial and fungal infection
Viral and opportunistic infection overview
Colonization versus invasive infection
Antimicrobial stewardship and contact precautions
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: infections, diagnostic testing, immunocompromised host
units.casePractice: A fictional febrile transplant recipient with papules: compare infectious and inflammatory causes and state isolation/escalation questions.
units.assessment: Test-selection exercise scored for differential breadth, sample choice, urgency and stewardship.

units.title: Cutaneous lymphoma, malignancy and complex systemic therapy
objectives: Recognize persistent atypical patches/plaques and understand why CTCL diagnosis may require serial clinicopathologic correlation.
Summarize multidisciplinary staging and treatment decision roles without treating a skin biopsy in isolation.
Relate cutaneous cancer treatment and malignancy-associated eruptions to the medical dermatology consultation.
topics: Mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome recognition
Biopsy and immunophenotype context
Advanced cutaneous malignancy treatment effects
Shared care with oncology/hematology
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: neoplasia, dermatopathology, treatment effects and consultation
units.casePractice: Fictional persistent rash despite two nondiagnostic biopsies: discuss repeat evaluation and referral; avoid declaring CTCL.
units.assessment: Clinicopathologic reasoning scored for chronology, sampling, differential, staging boundary and team handoff.

units.title: Complex wounds, ulcers, pain, itch and inpatient consultation
objectives: Assess wounds for cause, perfusion/infection/systemic context and current wound care without proposing unsupervised procedures.
Distinguish pressure/inflammatory/infectious ulceration and identify pathergy risk.
Develop a patient-centered consultation and communication plan for hospitalized medically fragile patients.
topics: Complex wound assessment
Pressure injury versus inflammatory ulcer
Pruritus and symptom burden
Inpatient documentation and handover
boardDomains: ABD CORE/APPLIED: common disorders, emergencies, communication and systems-based practice
units.casePractice: Fictional nonhealing ulcer with malignancy and immunosuppression: map evidence gaps and request interdisciplinary input.
units.assessment: Consult-note rubric: problem representation, differentials, safe next step, communication and patient goals.

units.title: Synthesis: evidence appraisal, uncertainty and board-style clinical reasoning
objectives: Integrate morphology, context, diagnostic tests and severity to rank a differential.
Appraise the date and evidence level of a treatment claim and check current specialty guidance.
Explain uncertainty, follow-up contingencies and limits of self-study.
topics: Case-based prioritization
Evidence updates and guideline caveats
Communication of diagnostic uncertainty
Learning plan and question review
boardDomains: Broad ABD CORE/APPLIED diagnostic and management domains; no independent CMD board examination/blueprint identified
units.casePractice: Final composite fictional case across units with timed 10-minute differential and written safe disposition.
units.assessment: Capstone rubric: diagnostic reasoning 30%, evidence and testing 25%, risk/urgency 25%, communication and limitations 20%.

assignment.title: Complex medical dermatology consultation portfolio
tasks: Write four fictional consult notes from original case prompts: immunobullous disease, cancer-therapy eruption, transplant-associated rash, and ulcer/purpura.
For each, provide a one-line problem representation, ranked differential, safety concerns, test plan, team handoff and evidence references.
Complete one short evidence update comparing a publicly accessible guideline/resource with a relevant lecture; flag date/version limitations.
assignment.caseStatus: All written case scenarios are fictional educational constructs. No authentic patient record or image is included.

assessment.format: Open-resource unit quizzes, case-note assignments, and final 10-question original self-test.
assessment.masteryThreshold: 80% proposed learning benchmark only; not validated, not predictive of board passing, and not an official ABD score.
assessment.remediation: Revisit the reading/lecture, state uncertainty, and reattempt a parallel original question.
assessment.safety: No clinical sign-off, procedure assessment, supervised case volume, accredited training, board eligibility, or certification.

studyHours.breakdown: 36.0 h verified specialty video floor plus 1.1 h separate foundations, approximately 18 h reading/evidence review, 12 h case/assignment work, and 4.9 h question review/reflection. A study plan only, not measured institutional workload.

mapping.name: BWH Complex Medical Dermatology Fellowship Program
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes fellowship for academic dermatologists in severe/complex disease, inpatient consultation, immunobullous disease, cancer-therapy adverse events, GVHD, dermatologic infections, complex wound care and multidisciplinary subspecialties. No public syllabus, rotations, didactic hours, case volume or accreditation claim found. Preserve this exact BWH institutional offering; no second institutional variant verified.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult develops tense pruritic bullae. Which diagnostic approach best supports distinguishing an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disorder from a drug-related mimic?

options.text: Use morphology alone and begin a definitive label.
Obtain appropriately sited routine histology and perilesional DIF, then correlate with clinical context and targeted serology.
Order a broad allergy panel without examining lesions.
Take a swab from an intact blister as the only test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Blistering disorders require clinicopathologic correlation. Routine histology and DIF answer complementary questions; targeted serology can support subtype classification. A single appearance or test should not be treated as definitive.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient receiving an immune checkpoint inhibitor reports rapidly progressive painful blisters and new oral erosions. What is the most appropriate immediate learning response?

options.text: Reassure because cutaneous reactions are always limited to skin.
Promptly escalate for urgent clinician assessment, mucosal/ocular and systemic review, and communicate with the oncology team.
Advise the patient to continue without contacting the treating team.
Assume infection and prescribe an antimicrobial remotely.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Severe, blistering, painful or mucosal disease during immunotherapy needs prompt evaluation. This course does not direct medication holds or treatment; those decisions belong to the treating clinicians in coordination with oncology.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a photodistributed scarring eruption asks whether one positive autoantibody proves that the skin disease is lupus. Which response best reflects sound reasoning?

options.text: Yes; a serologic test alone proves the cutaneous diagnosis.
No; integrate morphology, history, examination, pathology when indicated, and systemic evaluation with the appropriate clinicians.
No further work-up is ever needed if an antibody is negative.
Treat the laboratory result without assessing the eruption.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Serology is one component. Morphology and clinicopathologic correlation matter, and potential systemic disease requires proportionate evaluation rather than a single-test conclusion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A medically complex patient has palpable purpura and new hematuria. Which feature most changes the urgency and breadth of evaluation?

options.text: The purpura is limited to the lower legs.
Possible extracutaneous organ involvement, including renal findings.
The patient reports mild itch.
The lesions are not cosmetically concerning.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Skin findings may indicate systemic vasculitis; hematuria is a red flag for possible renal involvement and calls for urgent coordinated assessment. Skin morphology alone cannot establish a vasculitis subtype.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with extensive psoriasis reports joint stiffness and fatigue. Which assessment best matches a complex medical dermatology approach?

options.text: Record only body surface area and ignore symptoms.
Document extent, special sites, symptoms, functional impact and goals, then screen for comorbidity and coordinate evaluation of joint symptoms.
Use PASI alone as a routine clinical treatment mandate.
Assume joint symptoms are unrelated.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Severity assessment is multidimensional and psoriasis has important comorbidities. AAD notes different tools have different roles; PASI is primarily used in clinical trials rather than routine clinical practice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation develops a widespread eruption. Which statement is safest?

options.text: Any rash after transplant is diagnostic of cutaneous GVHD.
Consider GVHD alongside infection, medication eruption and other transplant-related conditions; interpret findings with transplant-team context.
Biopsy always settles the diagnosis without clinical context.
Exclude infection because the patient has a rash.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Transplant context raises GVHD but does not make it pathognomonic. Infection and medication-related mimics matter, and pathology must be correlated with clinical timing and team input.

practiceQuestions.stem: A persistent patch/plaque eruption has two prior nondiagnostic biopsies but continues to evolve. Which next reasoning step is most appropriate?

options.text: Declare cutaneous lymphoma without confirmation.
Reassess chronology and morphology, review prior pathology and consider repeat clinicopathologic evaluation/referral.
Assume that a negative biopsy rules out all future concern.
Use a single immunostain as a stand-alone diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Persistent atypical eruptions may require serial evaluation. CTCL assessment uses clinical and pathologic context; this educational course does not establish diagnosis or staging.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hospitalized immunocompromised patient has fever and new papules. Which approach is best before assigning the eruption to an inflammatory diagnosis?

options.text: Ignore infection because papules are nonspecific.
Review host risks and acuity, examine distribution/morphology, consider infection and inflammatory alternatives, and select testing linked to the differential.
Order every laboratory test without a clinical question.
Use a photo alone as definitive diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: In medically complex patients, infection may be atypical and inflammatory mimics are common. Clinical context should drive proportional testing and escalation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newly developed eruption appears after a patient started several medications, one recently discontinued. What history is most useful?

options.text: Only the medication list from today.
A dated exposure timeline covering prescriptions, OTC agents, infusions, starts, dose changes and discontinuations.
Only known allergies.
No medication history if the eruption is itchy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Drug causality depends on chronology and phenotype. Include recently stopped drugs and all relevant exposures; avoid assuming causation solely from temporal association.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the board credential relationship for this named fellowship?

options.text: Completion guarantees an ABD subspecialty certificate in complex medical dermatology.
The ABD identifies CORE/APPLIED dermatology certification and lists three subspecialty exam pathways; no separate CMD board examination is listed on the reviewed official pages.
The ACGME fellowship listing itself creates a separate board exam.
A fellowship programme page proves board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABD exam information lists dermatopathology, pediatric dermatology and micrographic dermatologic surgery subspecialty exams; no CMD exam is listed. Programme participation does not itself confer certification or establish eligibility.

assignment.title: Occupational contact dermatitis evidence-to-action portfolio
tasks: Write a structured (fictional) exposure history and timeline; separate clinical diagnosis from occupational causation.

rubric.fullCredit: Correctly weighs irritant, allergic, mixed, endogenous and relevant mimics; no morphology-only certainty.
Task-based chronology, work/nonwork comparison, product/PPE and missing-information analysis.
Test indication/series justified; limitations and relevance explicitly separated.
Controls prioritized at source and compatible with task protection; clear, non-stigmatizing language.
Claims cited; privacy respected; uncertainty and professional boundaries clear.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional nurse develops hand eczema after frequent washing and sanitizer use. Patch testing has not yet been performed. What is the most defensible next step?

options.text: Diagnose occupational ACD based solely on job title
Take task-specific work and nonwork exposure history and assess both irritant and allergic causes
Prescribe gloves for all tasks without checking compatibility
Use a negative patch test to exclude every workplace cause

practiceQuestions.rationale: Wet work and cleansing can injure the barrier, but ACD may coexist. Occupational relationship needs a detailed exposure and temporal history; testing is selected based on the clinical question. [NIOSH; occupational hand review].

practiceQuestions.stem: An appropriately performed patch test is positive to an allergen. What additional step is essential before attributing current dermatitis to it?

options.text: Assume current causation because positivity proves exposure
Determine current exposure and clinical relevance from the job/product history
Treat every positive as an immediate IgE allergy
Repeat the test every week

practiceQuestions.rationale: A positive patch test demonstrates sensitization; relevance must be linked to current, past, or future exposure. [DermNet patch testing].

practiceQuestions.stem: Which test primarily evaluates delayed-type allergic contact hypersensitivity?

options.text: Skin-prick test
Patch test
Serum total IgE alone
Wheal-and-flare intradermal test

practiceQuestions.rationale: Patch testing is used to investigate delayed allergic contact dermatitis; prick testing addresses immediate hypersensitivity and is not interchangeable. [DermNet patch tests].

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with suspected occupational allergy has negative tests to a limited baseline panel, but a highly specific resin exposure is documented. Best interpretation?

options.text: ACD is impossible
The limited panel may have missed the suspected agent; evaluate targeted testing with an experienced patch-test clinician
The rash must be psychogenic
Increase unvalidated concentration at home

practiceQuestions.rationale: A negative result may reflect an untested allergen or other causes; targeted exposure-directed test selection matters, while nonstandard home testing is unsafe. [DermNet; BWH programme].

practiceQuestions.stem: Which pattern best distinguishes patch testing from a diagnostic test for irritant contact dermatitis?

options.text: Patch testing is designed to confirm delayed allergic contact hypersensitivity, not direct irritancy
Patch testing diagnoses every type of eczema
Patch testing is a skin-prick test
Patch testing should reproduce a workplace injury at full concentration

practiceQuestions.rationale: Patch testing evaluates allergic contact sensitization. Direct irritant injury is assessed through history/exposure and clinical reasoning, not by applying hazardous full-strength workplace agents. [NIOSH; DermNet].

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional laboratory technician improves during vacation but is also using a new topical medication and has stopped working overtime. What is the best causation conclusion?

options.text: Occupational causation is proven
The away-from-work response is supportive but confounded; collect more exposure/treatment timeline evidence
Nonoccupational exposures are ruled out
A disability decision is automatic

practiceQuestions.rationale: Work-related improvement is one element, but simultaneous changes weaken causal inference. Use the structured criteria and document uncertainty. [Occupational Hand Dermatitis].

practiceQuestions.stem: Which control is highest in the NIOSH hierarchy for a confirmed hazardous skin exposure, when feasible?

options.text: Gloves only
Worker education only
Eliminate the causal compound or exposure
Apply moisturizer while exposure continues

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIOSH places elimination above substitution, engineering, administrative controls and PPE; choose feasible controls with occupational safety expertise. [NIOSH recommendations].

practiceQuestions.stem: A relevant positive patch test to a glove additive is found in a healthcare worker. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell the worker to stop all patient care immediately without assessment
Coordinate product ingredient confirmation and a compatible alternative/control with occupational health and infection prevention
Assume all nitrile gloves contain the same allergen
Advise use of any glove labeled hypoallergenic

practiceQuestions.rationale: The test has to be tied to exposure, and substitution must preserve task protection and infection-control requirements; glove composition and job compatibility matter. [Occupational hand review; NIOSH controls].

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about a positive test with no plausible current exposure is most accurate?

options.text: It may represent past or uncertain relevance and requires exposure reconciliation
It establishes current occupational disease
It automatically changes an employee’s job fitness status
It proves systemic allergy

practiceQuestions.rationale: Patch-test positivity alone does not establish current relevance or occupational causation. [DermNet patch tests].

practiceQuestions.stem: Which credential statement is correct?

options.text: This fellowship alone confers ABD certification
Contact dermatitis has a dedicated ACGME subspecialty board exam
ABPM OEM certification is a distinct specialty credential with separate requirements; this fellowship does not grant it
Course completion guarantees board eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABD certification requires formal accredited training and examinations; ABPM OEM is separately defined. Course participation confers neither. [ABD; ABPM].

title: Comprehensive Neurology Fellowship
prerequisites: Intended for physicians who completed neurology residency or senior residents preparing for primary ABPN Neurology certification; not entry-level medical education.
Assumed: neuroanatomy, neurologic examination, basic neurophysiology/pharmacology, common internal medicine, diagnostics and evidence appraisal.

MGB eligibility requires ACGME/RCPSC neurology residency, ABPN/RCPSC primary board certification/eligibility and full MA license eligibility; these are programme requirements, not credentials supplied by this course.
No self-directed patient examination, diagnostic imaging interpretation, treatment, prescribing or procedure performance is included.
objectives: Construct a patient-centred outpatient history, localization hypothesis, problem representation and differential without overstating certainty.
Select and interpret common diagnostic tests in context, recognizing limitations, red flags and urgent escalation.

Reason across common adult general-neurology topics: headache, episodic events, vascular neurology, movement/FND, cognition, neuroimmune, neuromuscular, neuro-ophthalmology/otology, sleep and autonomic presentations.
Map to the public ABPN initial Neurology blueprint while distinguishing exam domains from eligibility, training accreditation and exam prediction.
Communicate uncertainty, safety-netting, accessibility and follow-up in a simulated academic ambulatory setting.
Appraise current authoritative sources and design a small ethical scholarship/QI question without patient data.

Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada (RCPSC) — primary specialty certification (alternative named by MGB)

boardStatus.primaryBoard: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) for US initial Neurology certification
boardStatus.status: This is a real institution-specific one-year post-residency clinical academic general-neurology fellowship, not a primary residency, combined adult-child residency, or ABPN-recognized subspecialty certification. ABPN lists recognized subspecialty exams separately. No separate Comprehensive Neurology board exam or credential was identified. The official RCPSC page describes a primary Neurology (adult and pediatric) certification examination, with written and applied components; it is not a fellowship-specific examination.
boardStatus.blueprintScope: Mapped to ABPN Neurology Certification Content Specifications for initial certification, posted 2025-12-16: 400 questions, 80% adult/20% child and two interrelated dimensions (neurologic topics and competencies/mechanisms). Unit mapping is educational, not a weighting equivalence.
boardStatus.eligibilityContext: MGB requires an ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited neurology residency graduate, primary ABPN/RCPSC certification or eligibility, and full Massachusetts license eligibility. ABPN eligibility separately depends on current board requirements. This course does not establish eligibility.
boardStatus.separateFellowshipExam: No separate Comprehensive Neurology fellowship exam was found. ABPN primary Neurology certification is a separate board exam; RCPSC separately describes a primary Neurology (adult and pediatric) written plus applied certification exam. Neither source identifies a board exam specific to this MGB fellowship. Subspecialty exams have distinct eligibility rules.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Independent self-study does not provide a medical degree, accredited residency/fellowship, supervision, competence, licensure, board eligibility, procedure authorization, or certification. Programme applicant requirements do not become course credentials. Verify current rules with ABPN/RCPSC and the programme; no passing outcome is promised.

officialProgrammes.name: Comprehensive Neurology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official GME page describes a new one-year academic clinical general-neurology fellowship. Most time is clinical, with graduated faculty supervision, longitudinal ambulatory general neurology, cognitive/behavioral, epilepsy, functional disorders, headache, movement and neuromuscular exposure; autoimmune, autonomic and MS electives; teaching and a scholarly project. Named sites: MGH, BWH Neuroscience Center main campus and Faulkner Hospital. No full schedule, case volume, full didactic catalogue or lecture-hour ledger is published.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham Neurology Fellowship Programs / Harvard Medical School context
officialProgrammes.name: Mass General Brigham Combined Comprehensive Neurology fellowship at HMS
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Exact programme label preserved. It describes the same one-year clinical academic general-neurology fellowship across Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital, Faulkner Hospital and Harvard Medical School. “Combined” here indicates the named institutional MGB/HMS arrangement; it does not establish an adult-child combined residency or dual specialty board. This page states “accredited in 2024” but names no accreditor; official MGB GME page does not establish ACGME accreditation, so no ACGME claim is made. Sample timetable is illustrative, not a complete schedule.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Official MGB sources establish a genuine clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory entry or research-only/nonphysician supplement. Scholarly project is one component but most of the year is clinical. Combined is retained as institutional naming only. Exact affiliating sites are preserved. MGB programme pages do not publish complete schedule, case volume or lecture hours; accreditation statement on fellowship site is unattributed to a named accreditor.
sourceCaveats: Public sources support clinical fellowship classification and broad curriculum but not full rotations, case volumes, didactics or lecture hours.
One programme webpage says accredited in 2024 without accreditor; official GME page does not establish ACGME accreditation. Accreditation remains unspecified.
Initial ABPN blueprint posted Dec 2025 is used; its separate continuing-certification blueprint is not substituted.
Two public videos have observed runtimes; Iowa lecture index is group restricted and AAN MS page showed unavailable; excluded. Recheck public availability.
Clinical recommendations evolve. Human clinical review not performed.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person develops sudden unilateral weakness and language difficulty 20 minutes ago. What is the safest educational next step?

options.text: Arrange routine follow-up next week
Immediate emergency stroke evaluation
Assume migraine because headache is absent
Wait for symptoms to recur

practiceQuestions.rationale: Sudden focal neurologic deficits are time-sensitive; this scenario warrants immediate emergency evaluation, not outpatient observation or a self-study treatment choice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A witness reports a brief collapse after standing in a warm room. The person had nausea and dimming vision, then rapidly returned to baseline. Which is the best reasoning approach?

options.text: Diagnose epilepsy from loss of consciousness alone
Use event chronology and witness details to compare syncope with seizure and other causes
Order antiseizure therapy without assessment
A normal EEG would exclude all seizure disorders

practiceQuestions.rationale: Transient loss of consciousness has a differential; history, witness description and recovery are central, and no single symptom or test is definitive.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient reports a first seizure-like event. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: One seizure by itself always establishes epilepsy
Witness history and event details are important to classification
EEG alone identifies every seizure cause
All nonepileptic events are voluntary

practiceQuestions.rationale: NINDS emphasizes detailed history and eyewitness account; a seizure does not by itself establish epilepsy, and nonepileptic events are not thereby voluntary.

practiceQuestions.stem: A sudden severe headache reaches maximal intensity within seconds. Which framing is safest?

options.text: Label it migraine without further assessment
Recognize a secondary-headache warning pattern needing urgent clinical evaluation
Reassure based on age alone
Wait to see if it recurs over months

practiceQuestions.rationale: Thunderclap onset is among important secondary headache patterns in the ABPN outline; it requires urgent clinician evaluation rather than routine reassurance.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best reflects current functional-seizure guidance as displayed by AAN?

options.text: Functional seizures are imagined and should be dismissed
The guideline is a current evidence-based resource for diagnosis and management
A normal test alone proves functional seizures
Functional and epileptic seizures cannot coexist

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAN page identifies its Dec 2025 practice guideline as evidence-based; diagnosis and care require appropriate clinical assessment, respectful language and source consultation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with progressive slowness and stiffness also reports constipation and orthostatic lightheadedness. Which concept is useful?

options.text: Neurologic disorders may include nonmotor/autonomic symptoms
Autonomic symptoms exclude parkinsonism
Tremor is required for Parkinson disease
One symptom confirms diagnosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: NINDS describes motor and nonmotor Parkinson disease symptoms including autonomic and gastrointestinal features; this combination is not diagnostic by itself.

practiceQuestions.stem: An older adult has a subacute behavioral change, impaired comprehension and gait change. What is a sound first reasoning principle?

options.text: Assume primary psychiatric disease from behavior alone
Build a neurologic differential using timeline, collateral, exam and appropriate testing
Use one cognitive screening score as definitive
Ignore potentially treatable causes if MRI is abnormal

practiceQuestions.rationale: A neurologic change requires clinical synthesis; the published mystery case illustrates a broad differential and test selection, not a one-finding diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has progressive symmetric proximal weakness and preserved sensation. Which next reasoning step is strongest?

options.text: Localize by integrating distribution, reflexes, tempo and associated features
Conclude myopathy from one feature
Assume sensory loss must be present in every neuropathy
Interpret any unreviewed EMG as definitive

practiceQuestions.rationale: Neuromuscular localization depends on the pattern and context; no isolated feature establishes cause, and diagnostic studies need qualified interpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the ABPN Neurology initial-certification blueprint reviewed here is accurate?

options.text: It is the same document as continuing certification
It is a two-dimensional blueprint and describes 80% adult and 20% child neurology
It certifies completion of a general neurology fellowship
It guarantees passing after 36 video hours

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPN initial specifications posted Dec 16, 2025 describe 400 items, two interrelated dimensions, and 80% adult/20% child neurology. It is not a fellowship credential or pass guarantee.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public university lecture archive lists many recorded neurology lectures but states access requires group membership or alumni status. How should this course treat its duration?

options.text: Estimate runtime from title
Count all listed items as free hours
Exclude until public access and runtimes are verified
Count each title as one hour

practiceQuestions.rationale: The University of Iowa index explicitly restricts access; unknown runtimes and group-restricted videos cannot count as accessible free lecture hours.

title: Headache Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced learner: completed medical school and neurology/related physician specialty training; designed for fellowship-level study, not for lay diagnosis.
Foundational clinical neurology, neuroanatomy, pharmacology, epidemiology, and evidence-based medicine.
No clinical privileges, medical license, patient access or procedures are offered or required for independent study.
objectives: Use UCNS published blueprint to organize knowledge and monitor domain coverage, without claiming a complete official curriculum.
Classify common and selected uncommon primary headache syndromes with ICHD-3 and state missing criteria.
Recognize secondary-headache warning features and discuss context-sensitive diagnostic reasoning and limits.
Compare acute and preventive therapies using current evidence, contraindication awareness, comorbidity, age/life-stage and patient goals.
Interpret medication overuse, high-frequency headache, specialty referral and longitudinal outcome measures.
Communicate diagnostic uncertainty and patient-centred plans, and appraise new evidence.

assignment.title: Longitudinal headache formulation and evidence note
deliverables: Two fictional, de-identified-style case formulations: one primary headache phenotype with frequency/medication diary; one secondary-headache red-flag case.
ICHD-3 criteria mapping with explicit positive, negative, and missing data.
Diagnostic reasoning note naming urgent alternatives, test rationale and limits without issuing patient-specific orders.
For one fictional treatment decision, compare a dated guideline/position statement with a second primary source and explain population limits.
A 5-minute oral handoff and a one-page patient-friendly explanation that avoids blame.

rubric.standard: Accurate criteria, missing evidence stated, competing diagnoses preserved.
Identifies red flags and articulates urgency/limits without false reassurance.
Uses primary/authoritative sources and distinguishes guideline, position statement, label and local practice.
Tracks days, disability, medication exposure, comorbidity and goals separately.
Clear non-stigmatizing explanation; respects patient autonomy, privacy and limits.

assignment.passRule: Formative rubric only; not validated for certification, board performance, patient-care competence or eligibility.

assessment.formative: 10 original multiple-choice questions with rationales, 12 unit assessments, case analyses and rubric-scored project.
assessment.summativePlan: Suggested self-study plan: unit quizzes and two synthetic-case oral writeups, with spaced review after 2–4 weeks. No official exam questions or examination simulations copied.
assessment.limitations: Not a validated exam predictor, accredited course, board-prep guarantee, competency assessment or clinical credential.

unitMap.text: Headache fellowship, certification, and evidence literacy
coveredTopics: Fellowship vs certification; board eligibility; evidence appraisal; uncertainty and bias.

unitMap.text: Neurobiology, trigeminovascular pathways, and headache epidemiology
coveredTopics: Trigeminal afferents; brainstem/thalamic pain processing; neuropeptides; central/peripheral sensitization; epidemiology.

unitMap.text: Structured history, phenotyping, and ICHD-3 diagnosis
coveredTopics: Attack frequency/duration; aura; disability; associated symptoms; ICHD-3 coding; headache diary.

unitMap.text: Secondary headache red flags and urgent triage reasoning
coveredTopics: SNOOP4/SNNOOP10; SAH; dissection/RCVS; CVST; infection; tumor; GCA; intracranial pressure disorders.

unitMap.text: Migraine with/without aura, complications, and differential
coveredTopics: Migraine without aura; aura; chronic migraine; status migrainosus; persistent aura; migrainous infarction; vestibular features.

unitMap.text: Tension-type headache, TACs, neuralgias, and other primary syndromes
coveredTopics: Tension-type headache; cluster and other TACs; hemicrania continua; paroxysmal hemicrania; SUNCT/SUNA; neuralgia; cough/exertional/sexual/NDPH.

unitMap.text: Diagnostic testing and interpretation
coveredTopics: Imaging modalities; LP context; pressure disorders; temporal arteritis; sleep and other testing; incidental findings.

unitMap.text: Acute migraine therapeutics and emergency care
coveredTopics: NSAIDs/acetaminophen; triptans; gepants; ditans; antiemetics; nonoral routes; ED parenteral treatments; medication interactions.

unitMap.text: Preventive migraine therapeutics and chronic migraine
coveredTopics: CGRP mAbs/gepants; topiramate, beta-blockers, tricyclics and other established classes; onabotulinumtoxinA; outcomes; adherence.

unitMap.text: Medication overuse, complex refractory disease, and advanced care
coveredTopics: MOH; detoxification/withdrawal evidence; status migrainosus; procedures; nerve blocks; neuromodulation; inpatient care; refractory headache.

unitMap.text: Pediatric, pregnancy, women’s health, older adult, and comorbidity
coveredTopics: Pediatric phenotypes/abdominal migraine; adolescent acute/preventive guidance; pregnancy/postpartum; menstrual migraine; older adults; sleep, mood, vascular risk.

unitMap.text: Behavioral, integrative, communication, research, and practice systems
coveredTopics: CBT/biofeedback/relaxation; lifestyle without blame; HIT-6/MIDAS; shared decisions; trial design; access/equity; telemedicine.

topicGaps: Only 0.8972 freely accessible physician/resident-level lecture hours with directly observed public runtime were verified. The 36-hour target is not met.

Searches identified many public patient/family Headache School recordings and Stanford topic headings, but those are not counted as specialist lectures; many linked runtime metadata were unavailable or not directly checked.
AHS CME on-demand recordings may require registration/membership or subscription; no gated recordings were counted.
The pilot script and 24 topic-gap production plans are not recordings; none has a rendered/verified runtime or public URL.

Uncovered/barely covered exam domains include dedicated epidemiology/comorbidity, headache anatomy/physiology, imaging/LP/test interpretation, TAC/cluster and secondary headache lectures, acute/preventive therapeutics, paediatric/pregnancy/older-adult special populations, procedures/advanced therapy, and research methods.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: Primary ABMS/RCPSC/AOA specialty certification (eligibility prerequisite in the UCNS pathways)
American Board of Headache Medicine (ABHM) certification examination (separate organization; explicitly not ABMS-recognized)
medical.boardStatus: A formal UCNS subspecialty certification exam exists. The official UCNS page checked 2026-10-07 lists a 4-hour, 200-question exam and a 2026 exam schedule; biennial even-year administration is stated. The separate ABHM website describes a written plus oral/practical exam and expressly says ABHM is not recognized by ABMS. UCNS and ABHM are different credentials. Headache Medicine is not a standalone ABPN primary specialty board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Educational course completion confers no exam eligibility. Current UCNS criteria (updated 2025-12-11) require primary board certification by ABMS/RCPSC/AOA (with specified alternate faculty pathway), unrestricted active physician licensure, and one of UCNS-defined pathways. Its accredited fellowship pathway requires successfully completing a >=12-month UCNS-accredited headache fellowship and applying within stated limits. The BWH page says its own applicants need an ACGME/RCPSC-accredited residency, primary ABMS/RCPSC board certified/eligible and Massachusetts licensure. Confirm current criteria directly with the certifier; no eligibility promise.

officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a one-year UCNS-accredited clinical physician fellowship (since 2008), clinical care of migraine/headache/facial pain; sites at BWH Faulkner/Graham Center, 850 Boylston St (including Osher Center and Fish Center for Women’s Health), Massachusetts General Hospital and Children’s Hospital; thrice-monthly formal didactics, monthly case conferences, weekly division meetings, encouraged local/national meetings; integrated research and fellows-as-teachers. This is institutional information, not a released full lecture syllabus, case volume, or hour total.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The exact supplied item is a physician clinical fellowship, not a generic listing or research/non-physician course. “Combined” is the institution’s MGB/Harvard Medicine partnership/name, not a combined specialty or combined board. Clinical sites include a children’s hospital but this is not evidence of a separate pediatric headache fellowship or pediatric board. ACGME’s neurology requirements are residency requirements, distinct from this UCNS-accredited fellowship. No other variant was verified; only the BWH/MGB-Harvard combined programme is retained.
sourceCaveats: UCNS examination content outline linked here is marked revised 2020-05-22; blueprint remains the published source located during research and may change.

AHS red-flags summary is dated 2021 and itself warns it may not reflect later developments; the SNNOOP10 review identifies evidence and validation limitations.
BWH public curriculum page reports frequency and sites but does not provide complete fellowship lecture materials, fellow case volume, or full rotation requirements.
No human clinical review performed. Education is independent and unaffiliated; it does not grant accredited training, licensure, eligibility, competence, certification or guaranteed board passage.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has 6 untreated attacks lasting 6–12 hours, with unilateral pulsating moderate–severe pain worsened by stairs and nausea. Which best fits ICHD-3 migraine without aura?

options.text: Meets the core criteria, assuming no better alternative diagnosis
Does not qualify unless aura occurs
Requires at least 15 headache days/month
Cannot be diagnosed without abnormal MRI

practiceQuestions.rationale: At least five attacks, 4–72 h, two pain qualities/activity aggravation and nausea or photo/phonophobia; aura is not required.

practiceQuestions.stem: A new headache reaches maximal intensity within seconds during exertion. What is the safest next conceptual step?

options.text: Classify as primary exertional headache immediately
Promptly evaluate for secondary causes before assigning a primary thunderclap syndrome
Treat response to NSAID as proof of primary headache
Reassure because exertion-associated headache is common

practiceQuestions.rationale: Sudden thunderclap onset is a red flag requiring urgent diagnostic assessment; response to a drug does not exclude a secondary cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a pre-existing migraine disorder reports headache on 18 days/month and acute medication use above the relevant ICHD-3 overuse threshold for >3 months. Which coding principle is most accurate?

options.text: Replace migraine diagnosis with MOH
Consider both chronic migraine and MOH if each set of criteria is fulfilled
MOH requires opioid use
MOH is diagnosed after any one month of acute medication use

practiceQuestions.rationale: ICHD-3 says both underlying headache and MOH should be coded when both criteria are met; overuse thresholds vary by medication class.

practiceQuestions.stem: A transient visual symptom gradually spreads over several minutes and resolves, followed by headache. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: That timing alone proves migraine aura and rules out vascular causes
Gradual positive spreading symptoms can support aura, but new or atypical focal symptoms still require clinical assessment
Aura must last longer than 24 hours
All transient monocular visual loss is migraine

practiceQuestions.rationale: Aura features are assessed against ICHD-3; atypical, first, abrupt or negative deficits warrant a differential, not automatic attribution.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the correct blueprint weighting in the retrieved UCNS exam outline?

options.text: Treatment 10%, diagnosis 30%
Epidemiology/comorbidity 10%, anatomy/physiology 20%, classification/diagnosis 20%, evaluation/testing 20%, treatment 30%
All five domains 20%
Imaging alone 30%

practiceQuestions.rationale: The UCNS outline provides those five percentage weights (revised 2020).

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes UCNS Headache Medicine certification from a primary specialty board?

options.text: UCNS exam alone grants ABMS neurology board status
UCNS maintains a separate subspecialty exam; eligibility includes primary-board status and other pathway-specific criteria
The BWH fellowship itself is a board exam
All headache certificates are ABMS-recognized

practiceQuestions.rationale: UCNS certification is a separate subspecialty credential; the 2025 criteria specify primary-board and licensure prerequisites.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public list includes a headache fellowship and a generic neurology residency. What supports classifying the former as a clinical physician fellowship rather than a research-only postdoc?

options.text: Its name contains “fellowship”
Official programme page describes a one-year clinical programme, patient-care sites, clinical rotations and physician eligibility requirements
It is listed in a web directory
It publishes research

practiceQuestions.rationale: Institutional page supplies specific evidence of physician training; directory labels alone cannot establish this distinction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner considers prescribing a preventive for a pregnant patient based on a general adult migraine lecture. What is the best answer?

options.text: Use the lecture’s standard adult recommendation unchanged
Use current pregnancy-specific authoritative references and an individualized licensed clinician’s assessment; lecture alone is insufficient
Avoid discussing risks and benefits
Assume all migraine treatments are contraindicated

practiceQuestions.rationale: Special-population care requires current disease/drug-specific evidence and patient context; independent study is not clinical authorization.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately characterizes AHS guidance as checked on 2026-10-07?

options.text: No 2026 adult migraine prevention guideline exists
AHS lists an adult pharmacologic prevention guideline first published 2026-08-31 and an acute ED parenteral therapy update first published 2025-12-01
The 2016 ED assessment is the only current resource
All guidelines are formal FDA labeling

practiceQuestions.rationale: The live AHS guideline index lists these dates. Check the full guidance and drug labels for clinical use.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most defensible use of a public patient-facing headache webinar in specialist curriculum?

options.text: Count it as fellowship didactic time regardless of level or runtime
Use it as optional accessible contextual material, but do not count it as board-level lecture hours unless level, free access and runtime are directly verified
Rehost the video and transcript
Assume free viewing grants redistribution rights

practiceQuestions.rationale: The public access page and educational level matter; free-to-view does not confer copyright or redistribution rights.

title: Clinical Fellowship in Dementia
level: Supplementary clinical physician fellowship-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Physician-level learners with completed neurology or related residency; a medical student or public learner should use introductory resources and must not treat this course as professional qualification.
Working knowledge of neurologic examination, neuroanatomy, internal medicine, psychiatry, pharmacology, research methods and clinical ethics.

Comfort reading cognitive screening and neuropsychological test reports, MRI/CT/PET reports, basic statistics and clinical guidelines. This course does not teach or authorize independent diagnosis or prescribing.
objectives: Construct a patient-centered syndrome-level formulation that separates cognitive functional status, cognitive-behavioral syndrome, likely etiology and contributing comorbidity.
Use collateral history and longitudinal function to distinguish normal aging, subjective cognitive concerns, MCI, dementia, delirium and psychiatric/sleep/medical mimics.
Choose staged laboratory, structural imaging, neuropsychological and biomarker testing rather than indiscriminate testing; communicate uncertainty and incidental/mixed pathology.
Compare Alzheimer disease, Lewy body disease, frontotemporal lobar degeneration, vascular cognitive impairment and other common/urgent mimics using published criteria and calibrated confidence.
Interpret biomarker evidence in its intended symptomatic clinical context; avoid treating a biomarker as a standalone explanation for an individual's symptoms.
Discuss current symptomatic and disease-modifying options, care planning, safety, capacity, caregiver support, ethics and research participation with shared decision-making.
Explain limitations of an independent self-study course, public video resources and non-validated practice questions.

assignment.title: Longitudinal dementia formulation and shared-decision conference
assignment.instructions: Using a publicly accessible teaching case linked below or an instructor-provided fictional vignette, submit an 800-1200 word formulation. Separate syndrome, functional stage, differential, contributing factors, test justification, risks/benefits of next steps, patient/care-partner goals, uncertainty and references. Do not download/rehost case images or patient data. Do not provide a real person's diagnosis or treatment advice.

rubric.proficiency: Clear cognitive-behavioral description and function/tempo; distinguishes symptom from etiology.
Plausible competing and mixed etiologies tied to positives/negatives; no unsupported certainty.
Tiered, decision-relevant tests with limits, consent and interpretation.
Patient-centered goals, caregiver context, safety and risk/benefit communication.
Current authoritative citations; lawful linking, no image/record copying.
Communicates uncertainty and avoids implying training, eligibility or individual advice.

assessment.format: Formative unit worksheets and 10 original single-best-answer questions plus final case conference.
assessment.passStandard: No validated pass mark or predictive validity. Suggested learner self-check: review any missed question and explain why each distractor is wrong; instructor may set local rubric thresholds.
assessment.notice: Questions are original educational items, not official examination content and not a board-passing predictor.

mapping.name: MGH Clinical Fellowship in Dementia
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme page calls this a non-degree program for MD/foreign-equivalent physicians who have completed a recognized neurology or related residency and are U.S. board-eligible/certified. No detailed public lecture timetable, total didactic hours, case volumes or complete rotations are disclosed. boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN), Neurology (primary specialty certification)
United Council for Neurologic Subspecialties (UCNS), Behavioral Neurology & Neuropsychiatry (separate subspecialty certification examination; not a dementia-only board)
American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN), Geriatric Psychiatry subspecialty exam (relevant to some clinicians, not dementia-specific)
medical.boardStatus: As checked 2026-10-07, ABPN lists Neurology and several subspecialties, but no dementia-specific certification exam. UCNS offers a Behavioral Neurology & Neuropsychiatry certification exam (200 MCQs, four hours, biennial in even years); it is broader than dementia and not ABMS member-board certification. The AAN Fellowship Directory listing for this exact MGH dementia fellowship reports 1-year length, ACGME approval Yes, UCNS approval No, Other Approval No. The MGH/MGB programme itself describes a non-degree clinical/research programme. AAN listing is an authoritative professional directory rather than the ACGME ADS record; its ACGME field was not independently confirmed against an accessible official ACGME program record. The UCNS content-outline PDF linked from the official certification page redirected to a sign-in wall and was not accessed.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Completion of this independent educational course does not confer eligibility for ABPN or UCNS examination. Eligibility depends on the individual certifier's current prerequisites, applicable core-board status, qualifying fellowship accreditation, training, and other rules. In particular, AAN lists this exact MGH program as not UCNS-approved; do not infer UCNS BNN eligibility from participation. Verify with the certifier.

officialProgrammes.name: MGH Clinical Fellowship in Dementia
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme page calls this a non-degree program for MD/foreign-equivalent physicians who have completed a recognized neurology or related residency and are U.S. board-eligible/certified. It describes mentored MGH Memory Disorders Unit clinic one half-day per week, additional Frontotemporal Disorders Unit and Lewy Body Dementia Clinic exposure, weekly case/consensus conferences, Grand Rounds and inpatient encounters, plus mentor-guided research. No detailed public lecture timetable, total didactic hours, case volumes or complete rotations are disclosed. AAN Fellowship Directory calls it one year and reports ACGME approval Yes, UCNS No, other approval No. The sources' programme labels and directory accreditation fields are not interchangeable; independent official ACGME confirmation was not available in this check.

officialProgrammes.institution: Massachusetts General Hospital / Harvard Medical School (listed by MGB Neurology Fellowships)
officialProgrammes.name: Clinical Fellowship in Dementia (Memory Disorders Clinical Research)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Institutional variant page repeats non-degree, clinical and research framing and identifies MGH/Harvard Medical School. It describes same weekly half-day mentored memory clinic, FTD and Lewy body clinic exposure, conferences, Grand Rounds and inpatient exposure; it requires MD/foreign equivalent, completion of neurology or related residency, U.S. board eligibility/certification. It also lists USMLE documentation in application material. This is the same program, not a second independent specialty.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact track verified as a named MGH clinical physician fellowship with combined clinical exposure and research, not a generic directory category or research-only postdoctoral job. The programme is explicitly non-degree and post-residency; AAN says one year and ACGME approval Yes, but no detailed public curriculum or official ACGME database record was verified. It is separate from a generic Behavioral Neurology & Neuropsychiatry fellowship. It is not itself a board exam or a dementia-only certifying specialty. The second official URL is a variant description of the same MGH program.
sourceCaveats: Human clinical review was not performed. Content is independent self-study, not clinical advice, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence or certification.

Institutional pages describe programme aims, not a complete curriculum or guaranteed case volume. AAN directory reports ACGME approval Yes while the MGH page uses non-degree programme language; exact ACGME ADS record not independently verified, so the discrepancy is preserved.

ABPN does not list a dementia-only exam. UCNS does offer broad Behavioral Neurology & Neuropsychiatry certification, but the AAN directory reports this specific MGH fellowship as UCNS not approved. The UCNS content outline was login-gated; no blueprint domain weights have been inferred.
Clinical guidance and FDA labels change. Therapeutic decisions require current official label, specialist judgment, patient-specific risk assessment and local protocols.

The linked FDA lecanemab PDF could not be text-extracted in this session; it is supplied only as an official further-reading link. Re-check the current product label for all treatment specifics before any clinical use.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person reports increased forgetfulness, but no collateral history or function has been assessed. What is the best next step in a structured evaluation?

options.text: Label Alzheimer dementia based on the complaint
Obtain patient-centered history, informant evidence and functional assessment before formulating syndrome and likely cause
Order every available biomarker panel
Use one cognitive screening score as the etiologic diagnosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: DETeCD-ADRD recommends a tiered, patient-centered workup that establishes functional status, syndrome and likely cause using patient/informant history. A symptom or screening score alone is not an etiologic diagnosis; indiscriminate testing is discouraged.

practiceQuestions.stem: A specialty memory clinic is evaluating a patient with objective cognitive impairment. Under the 2025 Alzheimer's Association blood-biomarker guidance, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Any blood biomarker can replace clinical evaluation in all settings
A high-sensitivity test may be used conditionally for triage; confirmatory use requires both high sensitivity and specificity thresholds specified by the guideline
Positive tests should be ignored unless dementia is severe
The guideline recommends screening asymptomatic adults

practiceQuestions.rationale: The specialty-care guideline conditionally suggests high-sensitivity tests for triage (>90% sensitivity, >75% specificity) and high-sensitivity/high-specificity tests for confirmation (>90% each), with low-certainty evidence. It is not an unrestricted screening recommendation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has cognitive impairment interfering with everyday independence, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, cognitive fluctuations, parkinsonism and reported dream enactment. What is the most appropriate reasoning?

options.text: One symptom proves DLB
Assess against DLB criteria; these features are core clinical clues, while alternative and mixed pathologies remain possible
A positive amyloid biomarker excludes DLB
Hallucinations establish primary psychiatric illness

practiceQuestions.rationale: DLB criteria require a dementia syndrome and weigh core clinical features and indicative biomarkers; mixed pathology is common, so no single clue is a standalone proof.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which additional elements distinguish probable from possible behavioral-variant FTD under the revised FTDC criteria?

options.text: A positive amyloid PET alone
Significant functional decline and imaging consistent with bvFTD, in addition to criteria for possible bvFTD
Any one personality change
A family member's suspicion without progressive decline

practiceQuestions.rationale: Probable bvFTD requires possible bvFTD criteria plus significant functional decline and imaging consistent with bvFTD. The behavioral features must be persistent/recurrent and progressive decline established.

practiceQuestions.stem: A cognitively unimpaired person asks for a biomarker test to determine whether they will develop Alzheimer dementia. What is the most appropriate response based on the 2024 criteria overview?

options.text: Routine testing is recommended for all older adults
The criteria advise against clinical biomarker testing of cognitively unimpaired individuals outside observational or therapeutic research at present
A blood test guarantees future clinical disease
A normal screen excludes future pathology

practiceQuestions.rationale: The criteria overview states that clinical biomarker use is for symptomatic individuals, not cognitively unimpaired people outside research, and that disease-targeted therapy is not approved for cognitively unimpaired people.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with gradually progressive cognitive symptoms has a high burden of vascular MRI changes. Which interpretation is most defensible?

options.text: MRI white-matter changes always explain the entire cognitive syndrome
Integrate lesion pattern, timeline, examination and other etiologies; mixed causes may contribute
Vascular changes exclude Alzheimer pathology
No collateral history is needed

practiceQuestions.rationale: Cognitive impairment is often multifactorial. Structural imaging informs but does not independently establish a complete clinical explanation; the tiered formulation should consider vascular and degenerative contributors.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which feature should most strongly change the urgency and breadth of evaluation compared with a typical years-long gradual decline?

options.text: Subacute or rapidly progressive cognitive change
A stable lifelong preference for routine
A single missed name
A screening test performed in a non-native language

practiceQuestions.rationale: Atypical, rare or rapidly progressive presentations warrant specialist assessment and targeted testing; the DETeCD-ADRD guideline describes tiers of specialized testing and warns against indiscriminate shotgun workups.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the MGH Clinical Fellowship in Dementia most closely matches its public institutional description?

options.text: A public MOOC that independently qualifies a learner for board certification

practiceQuestions.stem: A course creator wants to reuse a published dementia case image because the article is free to read and states the patient details were disguised. What should they do?

options.text: Copy it because free access always allows reuse
Link to the article; verify its specific license/permission before reproducing, and do not copy patient records or images without rights
Remove the citation and use it
Assume de-identification removes copyright

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-read does not mean permission to reproduce. The case article states details were disguised, but reuse remains governed by the article's rights. Link rather than rehost absent a verified license/permission.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet entry is a clinical physician fellowship specialty label and actual programme discovery; not a generic directory category, research-only fellowship, or non-physician supplement. Two distinct institutional offerings are preserved (Mass Eye and Ear/MGB and Johns Hopkins Wilmer). MEE exact Anterior Segment source URL now resolves to a general hospital page; the Harvard Ophthalmology page lists that label. MGB describes Cornea, External Disease, and Refractive Surgery. Wilmer describes Cornea and External Disease. The labels are related clinical cornea/anterior-segment fellowships but are not silently treated as identical curricula. MGB says AUPO-FCC-certified; that is programme compliance certification, not a separate board. Johns Hopkins public page describes clinical fellowship and optional research-focused 2-year track; no public accreditation certification established here.

title: Ocular Oncology Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Advanced post-MD/DO independent self-study for ophthalmologists/fellows; not entry-level patient instruction.
required: Basic oncology, pathology and genetics literacy
Ability to read primary clinical guidance critically
prerequisites.sequence: 12 units; each has original source-backed study plans, case reasoning, assessments and unit objectives. Suggested 90 hours of independent study plus, if produced and watched, 36 planned video hours. These are plans, not verified viewing/training hours; active study may take more or less.

objectives: Localize ocular and adnexal tumors and recognize when urgent subspecialty evaluation is warranted.
Synthesize examination, imaging, pathology, staging, genetics and uncertainty in tumor-board-style discussion.
Explain the distinct reasoning frameworks for uveal melanoma and retinoblastoma.
Describe high-level treatment categories and trade-offs while deferring patient-specific choices to the treating multidisciplinary team.
Use current disease-specific guidelines, verify dates and jurisdiction, communicate prognosis cautiously, and respect patient image/data rights.

units.title: Core ocular tumor triage and multidisciplinary frame
objectives: Classify lesion by compartment (adnexa, ocular surface, uvea, retina, orbit) and urgency.
State immediate vision-, globe- and life-threatening risks and the required specialty referral.

boardDomains: Ophthalmology core knowledge; clinical reasoning and communication
units.casePractice: Write a one-page referral triage note from a fictional referral; identify missing facts and uncertainty.

units.title: Ocular oncology examination and imaging literacy

Interpret lesion size, location, subretinal fluid, pigment and growth in context.
Explain measurement, image-quality and longitudinal-comparison limits.
topics: Anterior segment documentation; fundus drawings/photos; ultrasound A/B scan; OCT; UBM; MRI/CT indications; serial photography; imaging pitfalls.
boardDomains: Ophthalmic examination; diagnostic test interpretation; safety

units.title: Uveal melanocytic lesions: nevus, indeterminate lesion, melanoma

Explain why small uveal lesions may remain indeterminate.
topics: Iris/ciliary body/choroid; lesion evolution; orange pigment, subretinal fluid, thickness and ultrasonographic reflectivity; imaging; differential with metastasis/hemorrhage/inflammatory lesions.
boardDomains: Neoplastic disease; image reasoning; evidence appraisal
units.casePractice: Present a fictional serial follow-up timeline and defend what additional data would change assessment.

units.title: Uveal melanoma biology, pathology and prognostic communication
objectives: Distinguish anatomic staging from molecular prognostic testing.
