practiceQuestions.stem: A small pigmented choroidal lesion has no prior photographs. Which is the most defensible initial interpretation?

options.text: It is melanoma because all pigmented choroidal lesions are malignant.
It is certainly a nevus if the patient has no symptoms.
It may remain indeterminate; integrate expert examination, documented features, appropriate imaging, and longitudinal context.
Biopsy is mandatory before any examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI notes that small uveal melanoma may not be distinguishable from a nevus; careful examination by an experienced clinician is central. Avoid certainty from absent symptoms or pigmentation alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which collection contains findings the NCI PDQ says may help identify uveal melanoma?

options.text: Orange pigment, subretinal fluid, thickness >2 mm, and low internal ultrasound reflectivity
Leukocoria, proptosis, and corneal ulceration only
Elevated IOP alone
Any one symptom is pathognomonic

practiceQuestions.rationale: These are listed clinical features that may help; they are clues, not a stand-alone rule or pathognomonic test.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees optic-nerve enhancement on MRI in a child evaluated for retinoblastoma. What is the safest evidence-based statement?

options.text: Enhancement alone proves optic-nerve invasion.
MRI is never useful in retinoblastoma.
MRI can aid evaluation, but optic-nerve enhancement does not necessarily indicate involvement and needs cautious interpretation.
MRI replaces ophthalmic examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI PDQ states MRI can help evaluate extrascleral/extraocular extension, but enhancement does not necessarily indicate optic nerve involvement.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with suspected retinoblastoma needs detailed tumor mapping. Which evaluation is described by the NCI PDQ?

options.text: Only external photograph
Examination under anesthesia with maximally dilated pupil and scleral indentation, documenting tumors and seeds
Routine CT as the sole test
Histologic biopsy is always required for intraocular diagnosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI describes examination under anesthesia with full retinal inspection and detailed documentation; intraocular retinoblastoma is usually diagnosed without pathological confirmation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Bilateral or multifocal retinoblastoma most strongly raises which issue for the learning team to address?

options.text: A need for genetic counseling/testing discussion because heritable RB1 disease is possible
Proof that both parents carry RB1
Proof that treatment is unnecessary
A diagnosis of uveal melanoma

practiceQuestions.rationale: Bilateral/multifocal disease suggests heritable retinoblastoma and warrants specialist genetics discussion; it does not establish parental genotype.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which overarching treatment priority does the NCI PDQ state for retinoblastoma?

options.text: Vision preservation regardless of tumor control
Life salvage first, then eye/vision preservation where appropriate, while reducing late effects
Avoid multidisciplinary care
Use one modality in all patients

practiceQuestions.rationale: The PDQ lists eradicating disease to save life, preserving vision as possible, and reducing treatment sequelae; risk-adapted team planning is needed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description best distinguishes ABO board certification from ocular-oncology fellowship training?

options.text: The ABO lists a separate ocular-oncology board examination.
An independent online course grants ophthalmology board eligibility.
ABO certification uses written and oral exams after accredited ophthalmology residency; this review did not identify a separate ocular-oncology exam.
Fellowship automatically certifies all trainees.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO public pages describe a two-part ophthalmology certification process tied to accredited training; no separate ocular oncology exam is identified. Eligibility must be verified with ABO.

practiceQuestions.stem: A guideline page includes an image-rich guide that is password-protected because patient image consent cannot be established. What should course authors do?

options.text: Rehost images because the text is useful.
Use only material permitted for public professional teaching; otherwise link to public licensed resources and do not copy images.
Remove watermarks and share privately.
Assume all freely viewable images are public domain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Melanoma Focus expressly notes the guide is password-protected due consent concerns. Free access never implies redistribution rights; do not copy or rehost patient images.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects multidisciplinary ocular oncology care?

options.text: Ocular oncology only treats intraocular melanoma.
It encompasses eyelid, ocular surface, intraocular and orbital tumors and often requires coordinated expertise.
Every tumor requires the same team and treatment.
Tumor boards replace individual patient preferences.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The open ocular oncology review defines a broad anatomic scope and multidisciplinary approach; its 2020 pandemic context should not be treated as current general practice guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: When studying uveal melanoma surveillance, which practice best supports current evidence use?

options.text: Rely on a single old review without checking dates.
Apply cutaneous melanoma pathways unchanged.
Check current uveal-specific guideline updates and jurisdiction, and confirm decisions with responsible specialists.
Treat all molecular markers as certain individual predictions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Melanoma Focus notes updates through 2023 pathway and later 2025 publication, and uveal melanoma management differs from cutaneous melanoma. Individual decisions and jurisdictional protocols require current expert review.

title: Balance and Vestibular Disorders Fellowship
prerequisites: Medical degree and prior clinical training appropriate to learner’s own licensed/authorized role; this course does not supply such credentials.
Recommended background: adult/pediatric neurology and otolaryngology fundamentals, neuroanatomy, audiology, pharmacology, evidence appraisal and bedside examination.
Clinical examinations and repositioning/procedural techniques require in-person supervision, patient-specific safety screening and local authorization; watching videos is not competence.
objectives: Structure dizzy-patient assessment around timing, triggers, associated symptoms and safety features.
Recognize major vestibular presentations and distinguish hypotheses from validated diagnostic criteria.
Interpret bedside ocular-motor/vestibular findings and common vestibular laboratory tests with caveats.
Apply current open clinical guidance to adult BPPV and acute dizziness in its stated scope.
Use current consensus criteria for vestibular migraine and seek current consensus material for other disorders.
Communicate uncertainty, urgent referral needs, interdisciplinary pathways, evidence limits and source rights.

units.title: Vestibular symptom language, timing and triggers
units.prerequisites: Medical graduate-level clinical foundations; neurologic and cardiovascular history-taking.
objectives: Separate vertigo, disequilibrium, presyncope and nonspecific dizziness without relying on symptom adjectives alone.
Classify presentations by timing and triggers as acute vestibular syndrome, spontaneous episodic, triggered episodic or chronic persistent.
Construct a concise symptom timeline with auditory, neurologic, migraine, medication, trauma and fall-risk features.
topics: Vestibular vs non-vestibular symptom mechanisms
Time course, triggers, associated features, medication review
Safety screen for stroke, syncope, falls and sudden hearing loss
boardDomains: ABOHNS primary: history, examination and differential diagnosis (broad competency mapping, not a published vestibular blueprint)
ABPN neurology: patient evaluation and clinical reasoning (broad specialty overlap, not a vestibular exam blueprint)
units.casePractice: Compare fictional 15-second roll-triggered spells, two-hour spontaneous attacks and 36-hour continuous symptoms; justify the syndrome category and immediate safety questions.
units.assessment: One-page symptom-timeline abstraction plus 5-item retrieval quiz; score: 2 points syndrome, 2 trigger characterization, 2 auditory/neurologic red flags, 2 medication/fall review, 2 uncertainty statement.

units.title: Vestibular anatomy, physiology and clinical localization
units.prerequisites: Unit 1; basic neuroanatomy, sensory physiology and ocular-motor pathways.
objectives: Relate canals and otolith organs to angular acceleration, graviception and translational acceleration.
Explain vestibulo-ocular reflex and vestibulospinal contributions to gaze and posture.
Link observed nystagmus or oscillopsia to a physiologic pathway while retaining central/peripheral alternatives.
topics: Labyrinth, vestibular nerve, brainstem/cerebellar integration
VOR, ocular motor and postural pathways
Canal planes and otoconial displacement as a model, not a complete account
boardDomains: ABOHNS basic science/physiology
ABPN nervous-system physiology and localization; broad mapping only
units.casePractice: Draw an unlabeled labyrinth, annotate canals/otolith organs, then state what observations would and would not localize a lesion.
units.assessment: Annotated concept map and oral explanation, rubric: anatomy 3, reflex physiology 3, localization caveats 2, clear diagram 2.

units.title: Bedside ocular-motor and vestibular examination
units.prerequisites: Units 1–2; supervised-clinical skills are necessary before performing maneuvers on patients.
objectives: Describe fixation, spontaneous and gaze-evoked nystagmus, alignment, saccades, pursuit, head impulse and gait assessment.
Explain the HINTS components and the restricted population in which GRACE-3 recommends trained use.
Identify central signs and state a safe escalation/referral pathway without using HINTS as a universal dizziness screen.
topics: Exam sequence and documentation
Acute vestibular syndrome with spontaneous nystagmus vs other presentations
HINTS plus hearing screen and gait; central/equivocal results
Limitations of technique, context, training and examiner reliability
boardDomains: ABOHNS patient-care/data interpretation
ABPN neurologic examination and diagnosis; HINTS use must follow current GRACE-3 context
units.casePractice: Use published case videos only as linked materials; write a structured exam note for a fictional acute continuous case and flag findings that would trigger urgent stroke evaluation.
units.assessment: Observed standardized-patient checklist (not completed here); written interpretation scored for correct syndrome, correct HINTS population, limits, central red flags and disposition.

units.title: BPPV: canal-specific diagnosis and evidence-aligned care
units.prerequisites: Units 1–3; understand positional testing is a clinical procedure requiring training and patient-specific safety assessment.
objectives: Distinguish triggered brief positional symptoms from continuous spontaneous vertigo.
Match posterior-canal suspected BPPV with Dix–Hallpike and consider supine roll for horizontal-canal patterns.
Summarize AAO-HNS/GRACE-3 recommendations, avoid routine imaging/suppressants in typical adult BPPV when guideline conditions hold, and reassess persistent symptoms.
topics: Canalithiasis/cupulolithiasis models
Dix–Hallpike and supine-roll patterns; bilateral/multicanal variants
Repositioning versus diagnostic uncertainty, mobility/cervical constraints and referral

units.prerequisites: Units 1–3; basic stroke syndromes and emergency escalation knowledge.
objectives: Distinguish acute continuous vestibular syndrome from episodic vertigo and positional BPPV.
Apply current GRACE-3 recommendations in the stated clinical context, including central/equivocal exam follow-up.
Discuss stroke, toxic/metabolic, inflammatory and peripheral causes without treating one bedside sign as definitive.
topics: Posterior circulation ischemia and urgent stroke pathway
Vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis differential, hearing loss and ocular-motor signs
GRACE-3 imaging limitations and role of MRI/MRA after central/equivocal HINTS

units.casePractice: For a fictional patient with continuous vertigo, inability to walk unaided and direction-changing gaze nystagmus, create a differential and urgent escalation note; do not infer a final diagnosis from the vignette.
units.assessment: Structured decision memo with 10 points: syndrome and timeframe 2, central warning features 2, exam limitations 2, guideline-based next steps 2, safe communication 2.

units.title: Vestibular function testing and interpretation
units.prerequisites: Units 2–3; basic audiometry and quantitative test interpretation.
objectives: Describe what common vestibular test classes assess and the pathways they sample.
Distinguish tests of VOR, otolith reflexes, vestibular-evoked responses, positional nystagmus and balance integration.
Interpret a test in clinical context, stating technical caveats and why normal/abnormal tests do not alone close a differential.
topics: vHIT/head impulse, caloric, rotary chair, VEMP, VNG/ENG, posturography

units.title: Episodic auditory-vestibular disease: Ménière disease and mimics
objectives: Use attack duration, fluctuating auditory symptoms, audiometry and competing diagnoses to frame a Ménière differential.

Identify sudden hearing loss/neurologic features requiring prompt assessment and avoid overconfident pattern matching.
topics: Consensus classification access and date awareness

units.casePractice: Compare fictional spontaneous 40-minute recurrent episodes with fluctuating unilateral hearing/tinnitus to a migraine-featured episodic presentation; list confirmatory evidence needed and alternatives.

units.title: Vestibular migraine and episodic neurologic vestibular syndromes
units.prerequisites: Units 1–3; headache history and ICHD terminology.
objectives: Apply 2022 Bárány Society/IHS vestibular migraine criteria and probable category without broadening the qualifying symptom definition.

units.title: Persistent dizziness, visual dependence and chronic vestibular syndromes
units.prerequisites: Units 1–3; distinguish chronic symptoms from acute vestibular syndrome.
objectives: Build a differential for persistent dizziness that includes peripheral hypofunction, PPPD and non-vestibular contributors.

Select referral and further evaluation questions rather than inferring PPPD from chronicity alone.

assignment.title: Integrated case portfolio

unitMap.text: Vestibular symptom language, timing and triggers
coveredTopics: Vestibular vs non-vestibular symptom mechanisms
Time course, triggers, associated features, medication review
Safety screen for stroke, syncope, falls and sudden hearing loss

unitMap.text: Vestibular anatomy, physiology and clinical localization
coveredTopics: Labyrinth, vestibular nerve, brainstem/cerebellar integration
VOR, ocular motor and postural pathways
Canal planes and otoconial displacement as a model, not a complete account

unitMap.text: Bedside ocular-motor and vestibular examination
coveredTopics: Exam sequence and documentation
Acute vestibular syndrome with spontaneous nystagmus vs other presentations
HINTS plus hearing screen and gait; central/equivocal results
Limitations of technique, context, training and examiner reliability

unitMap.text: BPPV: canal-specific diagnosis and evidence-aligned care
coveredTopics: Canalithiasis/cupulolithiasis models
Dix–Hallpike and supine-roll patterns; bilateral/multicanal variants
Repositioning versus diagnostic uncertainty, mobility/cervical constraints and referral
Guideline scope: adults ≥18 and non-complicated cases

unitMap.text: Acute vestibular syndrome and central mimics
coveredTopics: Posterior circulation ischemia and urgent stroke pathway
Vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis differential, hearing loss and ocular-motor signs
GRACE-3 imaging limitations and role of MRI/MRA after central/equivocal HINTS
Acute symptom management and uncertainty communication

unitMap.text: Vestibular function testing and interpretation
coveredTopics: vHIT/head impulse, caloric, rotary chair, VEMP, VNG/ENG, posturography
Audiometry, asymmetric hearing and cross-specialty coordination
Test quality, calibration, age/comorbidity and discordant findings

unitMap.text: Episodic auditory-vestibular disease: Ménière disease and mimics
coveredTopics: Consensus classification access and date awareness
Audiometry and longitudinal symptom records
Vestibular migraine overlap, BPPV, vascular and other causes
Treatment guideline updates and patient-specific risk/benefit discussion

unitMap.text: Vestibular migraine and episodic neurologic vestibular syndromes
coveredTopics: Episode number/intensity/duration and qualifying symptom forms
Migraine history/features and exclusion requirement
Criteria overlap and vestibular stimulation may trigger migraine symptoms
Follow-up, outcome measures and guideline updates

unitMap.text: Persistent dizziness, visual dependence and chronic vestibular syndromes
coveredTopics: Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (criteria require a separate consensus source review before diagnosis)
Visual motion sensitivity, motion intolerance and functional impact
Comorbidity, anxiety/depression, medication, falls and sensory integration
Shared care and longitudinal assessment

unitMap.text: Bilateral vestibular loss, ototoxicity, aging and special populations
coveredTopics: Bilateral vestibular loss and multisensory balance
Ototoxicity and monitoring questions
Age, gait, neuropathy, vision, cognition and fall risk
Pediatric referral and different disease context

unitMap.text: Vestibular rehabilitation, function and outcomes
coveredTopics: Unilateral and bilateral peripheral hypofunction evidence
Gaze stabilization, balance, habituation and functional goals
Dosing varies by chronicity/laterality; safety/fall risk and supervised therapy
Interprofessional communication and outcome measurement

unitMap.text: Audiovestibular red flags, imaging and multidisciplinary care
coveredTopics: Vestibular schwannoma and CPA differentials; imaging indication is clinical-context dependent
Sudden hearing loss/vascular risk and other urgency signals
ENT, neurology, audiology, PT and emergency collaboration
Institutional training scope, board status, consent and privacy

topicGaps: Current dedicated programme curriculum/rotations for the named one-year MEE balance fellowship unavailable publicly; only historical description found.
No public vestibular/oto-neurology-specific board blueprint exists in sources reviewed; mappings are broad crosswalks to primary board domains, not exam-domain weighting.
Verified free public recordings counted: 4.25 hours; no playlists, repeated IDs, premium/member-only items or patient-exercise short clips counted.

Topic gaps for additional source-backed original recordings: comprehensive vestibular test interpretation, Ménière criteria and management update, vestibular migraine, PPPD consensus, ototoxicity, pediatric and older-adult differential, rehabilitation evidence, audiometry and temporal-bone/CPA red flags.
Original recordings in originalClipPlan remain planned, not produced, rendered, uploaded or available videos.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

officialProgrammes.institution: Harvard Medical School Department of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery / Mass Eye and Ear
officialProgrammes.name: Fellowship in Balance and Vestibular Disorders (Neskey-Coghlan Fellowship in Balance and Vestibular Disorders)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Current HMS page lists it by this exact name under clinical fellowship listings at Mass Eye and Ear. The HMS page also lists Fellowship in Neurotology separately. A 2014 MEE establishment announcement described the balance fellowship as one-year post-residency, ≥75% clinical training/patient care, with research/didactic/scholarly time; this is historical programme information, not a current detailed curriculum or current eligibility notice. Current dedicated public curriculum/ACGME status for the named balance fellowship was not found.

officialProgrammes.name: Vestibular and Ocular-Motor Oto-Neurology Clinical Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Separate exact institutional variant, not the Harvard/MEE fellowship or a combined track. Current page describes a one-year physician clinical fellowship requiring ACGME-accredited neurology residency, with tele-dizzy/ED consult, oto-neurology and neuro-otology rotations; it does not state ACGME accreditation of this named fellowship or a separate board credential.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The Harvard balance/vestibular clinical physician fellowship and Johns Hopkins vestibular/ocular-motor oto-neurology clinical fellowship are retained as institution variants under this shared curricular subject, while their distinct prerequisite specialties and training designs are preserved. The separate Mass Eye and Ear two-year ACGME Neurotology Fellowship is context, not silently merged into the one-year named Balance fellowship. None is the same as research-only/postdoctoral or non-physician training.
sourceCaveats: Harvard’s current programme list is official but sparse; detailed one-year/75%-clinical description came from a 2014 MEE announcement and is explicitly dated.
Current MEE GME page describes a distinct two-year ACGME Neurotology Fellowship; that accreditation cannot be imputed to the balance/vestibular programme.
Hopkins page describes a physician fellowship but does not state separate ACGME accreditation or board eligibility.
Board mapping is a transparent broad competency crosswalk; no public specialty-specific vestibular board blueprint or board for the named fellowship was identified.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient reports 10–20 seconds of spinning only when rolling to the right in bed. Between spells they are well. Which initial syndrome framing best fits the history?

options.text: Acute vestibular syndrome
Triggered episodic vestibular syndrome
Spontaneous episodic vestibular syndrome
Chronic persistent dizziness

practiceQuestions.rationale: Brief attacks reproducibly triggered by position fit triggered episodic vestibular syndrome; then test for a positional disorder such as BPPV. Symptom quality alone is not the preferred organizing framework.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has continuous acute dizziness with spontaneous nystagmus. An examiner with formal bedside eye-movement training is evaluating the patient. In which setting does GRACE-3 recommend HINTS use?

options.text: Every patient who reports dizziness, regardless of timing or exam
Acute vestibular syndrome with nystagmus, by a trained clinician
Brief positional spells with a positive Dix–Hallpike test
Any chronic imbalance without nystagmus

practiceQuestions.rationale: GRACE-3 limits HINTS to patients with acute vestibular syndrome and nystagmus when performed by trained clinicians. It is not a generic dizziness screen.
practiceQuestions.domain: Acute vestibular syndrome and HINTS indication

practiceQuestions.stem: In an appropriate acute vestibular syndrome examination, the HINTS result is central or equivocal. Which next step is supported by GRACE-3?

options.text: Reassure and discharge based only on a normal noncontrast CT
Use MRI/MRA to help distinguish central from peripheral diagnoses and pursue urgent stroke assessment as clinically indicated
Repeat HINTS at home the next day
Diagnose vestibular migraine without further assessment

practiceQuestions.rationale: GRACE-3 recommends MRI/MRA when HINTS is central or equivocal. This is a safety-oriented educational answer, not a patient-specific disposition order.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult has repeated brief vertigo triggered by lying back. Which bedside test is recommended to diagnose posterior-canal BPPV?

options.text: Dix–Hallpike test
Routine CT angiography
Romberg alone
Caloric testing as the sole diagnostic test

practiceQuestions.rationale: GRACE-3 recommends Dix–Hallpike for posterior-canal BPPV, and the AAO-HNSF guideline emphasizes accurate diagnosis and appropriate repositioning. Evaluate individual safety and alternative diagnoses.

practiceQuestions.stem: A positional examination shows a horizontal nystagmus pattern during head turns while supine. Which is the most defensible interpretation?

options.text: This alone proves posterior-canal BPPV
A horizontal-canal BPPV pattern should be considered and interpreted with a supine roll test and full clinical context
This excludes all central disease
This establishes vestibular migraine

practiceQuestions.rationale: Horizontal positional nystagmus prompts assessment for a horizontal-canal pattern, including the supine roll test; observed patterns must be interpreted with history, full exam and alternatives. Published cases illustrate diagnostic complexity, not universal rules.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which feature set matches the core 2022 consensus criteria for definite vestibular migraine?

options.text: One episode of nonspecific lightheadedness with no migraine history
At least five moderate/severe qualifying vestibular episodes, 5 minutes–72 hours, migraine history, migraine feature in at least half of episodes, and no better diagnosis
Any dizziness with headache, regardless of duration or intensity
Any isolated positional vertigo with family history of migraine

practiceQuestions.rationale: The consensus criteria specify at least five qualifying episodes of moderate/severe vestibular symptoms lasting 5 min to 72 h, migraine history and migraine features with at least 50% of episodes, not better explained by another diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with recurrent dizziness also reports fluctuating unilateral hearing symptoms. Which next interpretive step is most appropriate before assigning a named episodic vestibular diagnosis?

options.text: Assume Ménière disease solely from the symptom label
Characterize attack duration and associated features, obtain/interpret audiometry and assess competing causes including migraine and vascular disease
Use a single vestibular test as a definitive biomarker
Ignore auditory symptoms if vertigo is present

practiceQuestions.rationale: Auditory history and audiometry are material to the differential; no single symptom or test should replace consensus criteria and exclusion of alternatives. Sudden hearing loss or neurologic signs warrant prompt evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an adult with peripheral vestibular hypofunction, which statement is consistent with the 2022 rehabilitation guideline?

options.text: Routine saccadic or smooth-pursuit exercises are recommended as gaze-stability exercises
Vestibular physical therapy should be offered to adults with bilateral hypofunction; exercise plans and safety require individualization
Rehabilitation should be withheld from all patients with bilateral loss
A uniform exercise dose can be prescribed without regard to chronicity or fall risk

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline strongly recommends vestibular physical therapy for bilateral peripheral hypofunction and advises against using isolated saccadic/smooth-pursuit exercises as specific gaze-stability training; dose is qualified by population and evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient reports oscillopsia while walking and unsteadiness in darkness. Which is the best educational reasoning approach?

options.text: Conclude bilateral vestibulopathy from symptoms alone
Consider bilateral vestibular hypofunction among alternatives and correlate with objective vestibular testing, neurologic exam and medication history
Exclude vestibular disease because static balance is intact
Diagnose BPPV without positional triggers

practiceQuestions.rationale: Oscillopsia and imbalance can motivate evaluation for bilateral vestibular dysfunction, but symptoms are not diagnostic alone; test findings and alternatives matter.
practiceQuestions.domain: Chronic vestibular loss and test interpretation

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the named Harvard balance/vestibular fellowship from neurotology board certification?

options.text: Any one-year balance fellowship automatically confers ABOHNS Neurotology subspecialty certification

ABOHNS lists Neurotology as a subspecialty requiring accredited fellowship and assessment; the public materials do not establish that the distinct one-year Balance and Vestibular Disorders Fellowship is that ACGME pathway
There is a separate national vestibular-disorders board exam for all physicians
The Hopkins neurology fellowship establishes eligibility for otolaryngology board certification

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOHNS explains Neurotology subspecialty certification follows ACGME-accredited subspecialty training and assessment. The distinct Harvard balance fellowship was described in its establishment announcement as one-year post-residency; current public pages do not equate it with the separate two-year MEE ACGME Neurotology Fellowship.

boardNames: American Board of Ophthalmology (ABO) Written Qualifying Examination — general ophthalmology content outline; not a pediatric medical-retina or ophthalmic-genetics fellowship board.
medical.boardStatus: The current ABO WQE outline is a general-ophthalmology examination outline. It maps inherited retinal/choroidal disease in the Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors domain and retinal disorders/visual function in Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus. No separate ABO board examination for Boston Children’s Ophthalmic Genetics/Inherited Retinal Diseases / Pediatric Medical Retina Fellowship was established by the sources checked. Fellowship listing, accreditation, certification and licensure are distinct questions.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course confers no board eligibility, certification, fellowship credit, clinical privilege, licensure or credentialing. The Boston Children’s page lists residency/NBME-or-ECFMG/USMLE/Massachusetts limited-license application requirements; it does not establish ABO eligibility, ACGME accreditation or any board consequence. Verify current requirements directly with ABO, the programme and the relevant regulators.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School teaching hospital; Harvard Ophthalmology lists the fellowship under Boston Children’s Hospital/Mass Eye and Ear clinical fellowships)
officialProgrammes.name: Ophthalmic Genetics/Inherited Retinal Diseases Fellowship; Harvard trainee page labels it Ophthalmic Genetics/Pediatric Medical Retina Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page calls this a post-residency pediatric medical retina fellowship, one year with potential extension to two. It describes diagnostic acumen and management of pediatric patients with diverse vision disorders; broad pediatric retinal, syndromic and metabolic exposure; retinal/visual-function assessment including gene-based and other therapies; department-wide weekly didactic and patient-oriented conferences, subspecialty clinics, quarterly journal club, grand rounds, neuroradiology and pathology conferences; mentoring; and at least one relevant clinical or laboratory research project. The page does not publish a complete didactic syllabus, observed lecture hours, case/procedure volume, accreditation status, separate board exam, competency sign-off, or automatic equivalence to MEE programmes.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This packet owns only the distinct Boston Children’s Ophthalmic Genetics/Inherited Retinal Diseases clinical physician fellowship, also called Ophthalmic Genetics/Pediatric Medical Retina on Harvard’s 2024 trainee page. Harvard lists MEE Inherited Retinal Degenerations and MEE Medical Retina separately, and lists distinct fellows/directors for each; this record must not be merged with MED-X081 or MED-123. Institution/programme sources support programme facts only; clinical teaching claims are grounded separately in AAO, ISCEV, FDA, PMC and public educational recordings.
sourceCaveats: All programme facts were re-fetched from public Boston Children’s and Harvard pages on 2026-10-08. The public page does not establish ACGME accreditation, a separate fellowship board, ABO eligibility, licensure outcome, case volume, complete curriculum or automatic curriculum equivalence.

Clinical sources support educational reasoning, not a treatment plan for an individual. The AAO guideline is 2022; product labels and trial records can change, so current source checking is required in real clinical contexts.

Media duration/access evidence is reused explicitly from the current MED-X081 canonical ledger for identical public URLs/video IDs, then mapped to this distinct course. No unique source video is counted more than once within MED-X117. Direct public viewing is not a license to rehost.

originalClipPlan.title: Phenotype-first reasoning for a child with suspected IRD
objectives: Elicit age at onset, tempo, symptoms, family history and systemic clues without equating a family history with proof of an inherited disorder.
Create a differential that includes acquired, toxic, inflammatory, infectious, nutritional and vascular mimics; state a referral/escalation boundary.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: A child has slowly progressive, bilateral and broadly symmetric outer-retinal findings, but no known affected relatives. Which statement is the safest next inference?

options.text: The absent family history rules out inherited disease.
The pattern supports considering inherited disease, but phenotype-led evaluation and alternative causes remain necessary.
Symmetry proves a single-gene disorder.
Immediate trial enrollment is indicated.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Symmetry and slow progression can raise suspicion, but family history may be absent and non-genetic causes must be considered. A phenotype-led assessment comes before a molecular or treatment conclusion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional panel report identifies a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) in a gene unrelated to the child’s current phenotype. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: It establishes the diagnosis.
It establishes gene-therapy eligibility.
It requires cautious phenotype correlation and may need segregation, additional evidence or reanalysis.
It should be ignored permanently.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A VUS is not automatically disease-causing; interpretation belongs in phenotype context and may evolve as evidence changes. It is not a treatment-eligibility result.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which report detail is most necessary to compare a fictional full-field ERG result reliably with a prior record?

options.text: Only the diagnosis in the referral note.
Adaptation state, stimulus variables, representative responses, reference ranges and any protocol deviations.
The patient’s preferred frame color.
A single waveform without calibration.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ISCEV specifies reporting of conditions, waveforms, calibration, reference values and deviations. These are necessary for interpretation; an ERG alone does not name a disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a fictional young child with suspected diffuse photoreceptor dysfunction, which statement about ERG is best?

options.text: Adult normative values apply without qualification.
Pediatric recordings require age, cooperation, method and possible sedation/anesthesia effects to be documented and interpreted cautiously.
ERG must never be attempted in children.
An ERG result eliminates the need for clinical phenotype.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ISCEV standard emphasizes pediatric age-related waveform differences, cooperation and recording-method considerations. Local pediatric safety protocols govern any sedation/anesthesia.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the FDA indication stated on the Luxturna page?

options.text: All inherited retinal degenerations.
Any child with night blindness.
Patients with confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy.
Any participant in an IRD registry.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA’s product page states the indication as confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy. It does not make an individual candidacy decision or substitute for the full label and specialist evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional child with suspected macular dystrophy needs documentation of retinal structure. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: OCT alone proves the molecular diagnosis.
OCT provides cross-sectional structural information and must be interpreted with history, exam, other testing and longitudinal context.
Every imaging modality answers the same question.
Fundus photography is always risk-free and mandatory at every visit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO describes OCT as cross-sectional imaging useful for baseline and structural monitoring. The statement also describes modality-specific benefits and cautions, including sparing light exposure when useful in some maculopathies.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional pedigree appears autosomal dominant, but no pathogenic result has been obtained. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The pedigree is a molecular confirmation.
The pedigree can guide a hypothesis and counseling discussion, but it does not substitute for phenotype correlation and appropriately interpreted testing.
There can be no de novo event.
All relatives should be told they have a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pedigrees inform risk hypotheses, but variable expressivity, incomplete penetrance and de novo variation can complicate patterns. Results require careful communication and counseling.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional registry record is marked “recruiting.” What does that status establish?

options.text: The study is clinically appropriate for every person with a similar diagnosis.
The listed study is recruiting according to the current record; eligibility, location, criteria and risks still require review with qualified professionals.
The therapy is FDA approved.
The study has demonstrated benefit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ClinicalTrials.gov is a registry whose submitters are responsible for listing content. Recruiting status neither establishes personal eligibility nor proves benefit.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which task is appropriate for independent cognitive study but does not demonstrate clinical fellowship competence?

options.text: Performing a pediatric retinal procedure without supervision.
Using a fictional case to map phenotype, testing limitations and referral questions from cited sources.
Issuing a Massachusetts license.
Credentialing another learner for sedation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Fictional evidence-based reasoning is appropriate self-study. Procedures, licensure, credentialing and supervised clinical care remain external professional responsibilities.

practiceQuestions.stem: The Harvard trainee page lists a Boston Children’s Ophthalmic Genetics/Pediatric Medical Retina fellow and separately lists MEE Inherited Retinal Degenerations and MEE Medical Retina fellows. What is the safest catalog conclusion?

options.text: They are all one institutional variant.
The listings support separate named clinical fellowships; their curricula, accreditation and board effects must not be inferred from the names alone.
They share an automatic fellowship board exam.
The Boston Children’s page establishes MEE requirements.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The public Harvard page distinguishes the programmes by name, institution and director. It does not establish curriculum equivalence, accreditation or a separate board examination.
